title: Reading a Trace, Predicting a Drug

scenes.tts: One small step of current, one voltage trace. What can it tell you about the cell?
scenes.visual: A current-clamp step (top) and its smooth voltage response (bottom). The question appears.
scenes.narration: One small step of current, one voltage trace. What can it tell you about the cell?

scenes.tts: For a compact, passive cell, it gives three numbers.
scenes.visual: Three empty slots appear beside the trace: Rin, τ, C.
scenes.narration: For a compact, passive cell, it gives three numbers.

scenes.tts: First, input resistance: the plateau divided by the current.
scenes.visual: The plateau and step size are marked on the trace. Slot 1 fills: Rin = ΔV / I.
scenes.narration: First, input resistance: the plateau divided by the current.

scenes.tts: Second, the time constant: the time to reach sixty-three percent of the plateau.
scenes.caption: Second, the time constant: the time to reach 63% of the plateau.
scenes.visual: A flag at 63% of the plateau, with its time marked. Slot 2 fills: τ = time to 63%.
scenes.narration: Second, the time constant: the time to reach 63% of the plateau.

scenes.tts: Third, capacitance: the time constant divided by the input resistance.
scenes.visual: Slot 3 fills: C = τ / Rin.
scenes.narration: Third, capacitance: the time constant divided by the input resistance.

scenes.tts: The word compact matters. In a cell with big dendrites, that last step underestimates the capacitance.
scenes.visual: A compact round cell beside a branched neuron; a caution tag on the branched one: τ / Rin underestimates C.
scenes.narration: The word compact matters. In a cell with big dendrites, that last step underestimates the capacitance.

scenes.tts: Give several small steps below threshold. Plot each plateau against its current. The slope is the input resistance.
scenes.visual: Several hyperpolarizing steps of different sizes; their plateaus plotted as ΔV against I fall on a straight line. Label: slope = Rin.
scenes.narration: Give several small steps below threshold. Plot each plateau against its current. The slope is the input resistance.

scenes.tts: A straight line fits a passive membrane. But it does not prove one.
scenes.visual: Card beside the plot: straight line = fits passive, does not prove it.
scenes.narration: A straight line fits a passive membrane. But it does not prove one.

scenes.tts: Now check the trace's shape. A pure resistor and capacitor gives a smooth rise to a plateau.
scenes.visual: The smooth trace, labelled pure RC.
scenes.narration: Now check the trace's shape. A pure resistor and capacitor gives a smooth rise to a plateau.

scenes.tts: If the voltage overshoots and sags back during a hyperpolarizing step, a conductance is turning on with voltage.
scenes.visual: A second trace overlays: during a hyperpolarizing step it overshoots and sags back toward rest. Label: sag.
scenes.narration: If the voltage overshoots and sags back during a hyperpolarizing step, a conductance is turning on with voltage.

scenes.tts: Often it is the HCN current. And if the plot of plateau against current bends, input resistance depends on voltage.
scenes.visual: The sag is labelled HCN current (often). The V–I plot bends at one end.
scenes.narration: Often it is the HCN current. And if the plot of plateau against current bends, input resistance depends on voltage.

scenes.tts: Either way, a single resistor and capacitor fit will mislead you.
scenes.visual: A fitted single-exponential curve misses the sag trace. Label: single RC fit misleads.
scenes.narration: Either way, a single resistor and capacitor fit will mislead you.

scenes.tts: To predict a drug, ask two questions. Which ion's conductance changed, and which way? That moves rest.
scenes.visual: The voltage scale returns with its ropes. Question 1 card: which conductance changed? → rest.
scenes.narration: To predict a drug, ask two questions. Which ion's conductance changed, and which way? That moves rest.

scenes.tts: And did the total conductance go up or down? That moves input resistance and the time constant.
scenes.visual: Question 2 card: total conductance up or down? → Rin and τ.
scenes.narration: And did the total conductance go up or down? That moves input resistance and the time constant.

scenes.tts: A drug opens more potassium leak channels, and does nothing else. What happens to rest, input resistance, and the time constant?
scenes.visual: On screen: Pause. A drug opens more K+ leak channels. Rest? Rin? τ?
scenes.narration: A drug opens more potassium leak channels, and does nothing else. What happens to rest, input resistance, and the time constant?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; a small countdown ring runs.

scenes.tts: Potassium's rope gets thicker, so rest moves toward potassium's mark. The cell hyperpolarizes.
scenes.visual: The purple rope thickens; the marker slides left toward E_K.
scenes.narration: Potassium's rope gets thicker, so rest moves toward potassium's mark. The cell hyperpolarizes.

scenes.tts: Total conductance rises. So input resistance falls, and the time constant shortens.
scenes.visual: Before and after traces overlay: after the drug, the test step gives a smaller, faster response.
scenes.narration: Total conductance rises. So input resistance falls, and the time constant shortens.

scenes.tts: Closing a leak does the reverse. Input resistance and the time constant rise, and rest moves away from that leak's reversal potential.
scenes.visual: A rope thins; the marker slides away from that rope's mark; the test response grows larger and slower.
scenes.narration: Closing a leak does the reverse. Input resistance and the time constant rise, and rest moves away from that leak's reversal potential.

scenes.tts: One case surprises most students. Suppose the new channels reverse right at rest.
scenes.visual: Title card: shunting.
scenes.narration: One case surprises most students. Suppose the new channels reverse right at rest.

scenes.tts: Chloride channels do this when chloride sits at equilibrium. Their rope is anchored exactly where the marker sits.
scenes.visual: A green rope labelled Cl− is anchored at the marker's own position on the scale.
scenes.narration: Chloride channels do this when chloride sits at equilibrium. Their rope is anchored exactly where the marker sits.

scenes.tts: The rope is not stretched, so it adds no pull. Rest does not move.
scenes.visual: The green rope hangs slack; the marker stays put.
scenes.narration: The rope is not stretched, so it adds no pull. Rest does not move.

scenes.tts: But the marker is now harder to move. Any other current shifts the voltage less, and faster.
scenes.visual: The teal injected-current arrow pushes the marker; it moves less than before. The test response is smaller and faster.
scenes.narration: But the marker is now harder to move. Any other current shifts the voltage less, and faster.

scenes.tts: That is shunting. It lowers input resistance without moving the resting potential.
scenes.visual: Card: shunting = lower Rin, same Vm.
scenes.narration: That is shunting. It lowers input resistance without moving the resting potential.

scenes.tts: So here is the whole rule, for our passive model. With no injected current, and the pump's own current set aside, rest is where the leaks balance.
scenes.visual: The scale with all ropes, the marker at its balance point. Banner, first half: rest is where the leaks balance. Small label: passive model; no injected current; pump's direct current omitted.
scenes.narration: So here is the whole rule, for our passive model. With no injected current, and the pump's own current set aside, rest is where the leaks balance.

scenes.tts: And the leak, with capacitance and the core, decides how big, how fast, and how far a nudge goes.
scenes.visual: Takeaway card: rest is where the leaks balance; the leak, with capacitance and the core, decides how big, how fast and how far a nudge goes.
scenes.narration: And the leak, with capacitance and the core, decides how big, how fast, and how far a nudge goes.
